skills.summary: One abstract shape, built from squares, circles, bars or loops, that stands for the organisation with no letters. The shape implies a direction, growth or a cycle, and is strong enough to stand alone on a sign or a coin.

skills.name: Wordmark-led minimal
skills.thesis: The name is the mark: one carefully spaced word, with one detail of its own, is clearer and more durable than any symbol.
skills.summary: The name alone, set or drawn in one weight of a sans, with a single detail that makes it own: a cut stroke, a hidden arrow, a joined pair of letters. No symbol and no frame.

skills.name: Gradient 3D and glass
skills.thesis: On a screen a mark can be a lit object: gloss, depth and reflection make it feel new, touchable and alive.
skills.summary: A mark lit like an object: top highlights, gradients from light to deep colour, a glass bevel, a reflection under it and a soft drop shadow. The screen was now the main medium, and the mark imitated a polished button or a globe.
use_cases: app icons with a retro theme

skills.name: Flat 2010s mark
skills.thesis: On a screen honesty is flat colour: a mark is a set of clean shapes that read at icon size and scale with no loss.
skills.summary: The gloss goes away. A simple symbol or a geometric sans word in 2–4 bright flat colours, with no gradient, no shadow and no bevel, drawn to work as a 24 px app icon first.

skills.name: Pixel icon
skills.thesis: An icon is a set of square pixels on a fixed grid, and the grid is part of the look, not a limit to hide.
skills.summary: Icons drawn on a hard pixel grid, one square at a time. Each pixel is on or off, edges are stairs, and the set has 1 to 16 colours. The style began with low screen resolution and returns now as a retro choice.
use_cases: developer tools with a playful voice

skills.name: Isometric icon
skills.thesis: An icon can show an object as a solid in space and keep it exact, because parallel projection keeps every edge at a true angle.
skills.summary: Icons drawn as small objects in a parallel isometric view: three faces at once, edges at 30° to the horizontal, no vanishing point. Flat colour fills give each face its own tone.

skills.name: Skeuomorphic icon
skills.thesis: An icon is a small picture of a real object, and the material tells the user what the function is.
skills.summary: Icons that look like small real objects: leather, glass, metal and paper, with light from the top, gradients and a soft cast shadow. The style peaked with Mac OS X Aqua and iOS 1 to 6, and Tango gave it an open, semi-realistic form.
use_cases: brand illustrations with a tactile feel

skills.name: Flat icon
skills.thesis: An icon is a sign, not a picture, and flat shapes in clear colour carry the meaning faster than material and light.
skills.summary: Icons in flat, solid colour shapes with no gradient, no texture and no light model. A simple object sits on a coloured ground, often a circle or a rounded square. Flat icons replaced skeuomorphic icons in the early 2010s.

skills.name: Solid glyph icon
skills.thesis: An icon is a single solid mark, and a silhouette with cut-out details reads best at small sizes and on any ground.
skills.summary: Icons as solid, one-colour silhouettes, like the glyphs of a bold typeface. Inner details are cut out of the fill as gaps. The style began with icon fonts and stays the default for small, high-contrast UI.
use_cases: buttons and small UI at 12–16 px
active state of an outline set

skills.name: Outline icon
skills.thesis: An icon set is a typeface of objects: one stroke, one grid and one corner radius make hundreds of glyphs read as one family.
skills.summary: Icons drawn as one even stroke on a 24 px grid, with round caps and joins and no fill. The set reads like a light typeface: the same line weight, the same corner radius and the same live area for every glyph.

skills.name: Material Symbols
skills.thesis: An icon system is a set of tokens: one grid and four variable axes let one glyph serve every size, weight and state.
skills.summary: Google's open icon system: geometric glyphs on a 24 dp grid with keyline shapes. Material Icons (2014) gave five themes; Material Symbols (2022) is a variable font with axes for fill, weight, grade and optical size.
use_cases: design systems that need fill and weight states

skills.name: Duotone icon
skills.thesis: One colour in two strengths gives an icon a figure and a ground, so the meaning reads first and the detail second.
skills.summary: Icons in two tones of one colour: a main shape at full strength and a secondary layer at 20–40% opacity. The second tone gives hierarchy and a little depth, but the icon stays a flat glyph.

skills.name: 3D clay icon
skills.thesis: After a decade of flat glyphs, an icon can have volume again if the forms stay simple, round and soft like a toy.
skills.summary: Icons rendered in 3D with soft, matte, clay-like materials, large round corners and a soft shadow. They bring depth back after the flat years, but with toy-like simplicity and no real texture.
use_cases: landing page heroes and feature cards
consumer and fintech apps with a soft voice

skills.name: Blackletter
skills.thesis: A letter written with a broad nib held at a steep angle breaks each curve into straight strokes and makes a dark, even texture on the page.
skills.summary: The broken letter of the Gothic book hand: narrow, dark, with strokes that turn at sharp angles instead of curves. Gutenberg printed his Bible in textura; Fraktur stayed the German text face until 1941. Today it carries tradition, heraldry, metal and rebellion.

skills.name: Garalde old-style serif
skills.thesis: A text letter keeps the rhythm of the hand that wrote it, so the eye reads a page without effort.
skills.summary: The roman of the Renaissance book: moderate contrast, a diagonal stress from the broad-nib pen, bracketed serifs and a small x-height. It is the default text face of the long tradition and reads well for hours.

skills.name: Formal script
skills.thesis: A letter is one movement of a flexible pointed pen: pressure on the downstroke, a hairline on the upstroke, and every letter joined to the next.
skills.summary: Joined, sloped letters from the pointed pen of the eighteenth-century writing master. Pressure makes the downstrokes swell and the upstrokes become hairlines. It speaks of invitations, ceremony and romance, and reads well only in short lines.
use_cases: one signature line in a brand

skills.name: Transitional serif
skills.thesis: A letter can be drawn by reason and still serve the reader: the pen gives way to the engraver's line, but not yet to the extreme.
skills.summary: The Enlightenment roman between the old style and the Didone: the stress turns nearly vertical, the contrast rises, and the serifs become flatter and sharper. It is precise but still warm, and it reads well in text.

skills.name: Didone
skills.thesis: A letter is a geometric figure of thick and thin, cut as fine as the metal and the paper allow.
skills.summary: The extreme of the roman: a vertical stress, hairline serifs with no bracket, and a strong contrast between stem and hairline. At display sizes it is the voice of fashion and luxury; in small text it sparkles and tires the eye.

skills.name: Fat face display
skills.thesis: A letter for a poster is as black as the stem can be while the hairlines keep it readable.
skills.summary: The first type made only for display: a Didone pushed to extreme weight, with stems as thick as half the letter and hairlines kept fine. It shouts from posters and covers, and it fails in text.
use_cases: editorial hero titles on the web

skills.name: Slab serif
skills.thesis: A letter for a loud and busy world must be heavy, square and hard to break.
skills.summary: Heavy, square serifs on a sturdy letter with low contrast. Born on the poster in industrial Britain, it carries a loud, solid and practical voice, and modern text cuts serve screens and typewriters as well.

skills.name: Grotesque sans
skills.thesis: A letter without serifs is plain, and the plain letter is the strongest one at a distance.
skills.summary: The first sans serifs: plain, heavy letters for posters, with a little contrast, some quirks of width and a two-storey g. Later text cuts such as Akzidenz-Grotesk and Franklin Gothic gave the class a sober, workmanlike voice.

skills.name: Monospace
skills.thesis: When every character has the same width, columns align without a grid and each character is a unit the reader can count.
skills.summary: Every character takes the same width, as on a typewriter or a terminal. The narrow letters get serifs or wide arms and the wide letters are squeezed. It is the voice of code, data, forms and the typewritten document.

skills.name: Humanist sans
skills.thesis: A sans serif reads best when it keeps the proportions and the open forms of the written roman.
skills.summary: A sans serif on the skeleton of the Renaissance roman: open apertures, varied widths, a little stroke modulation and an angled cut on the terminals. It reads well at small sizes and in poor conditions, and sounds warm.
use_cases: product interfaces with a warm voice

skills.name: Geometric sans
skills.thesis: A letter is a construction of pure forms, free of the hand and of history.
skills.summary: A sans serif built from the circle, the square and the triangle: a round o, a single-storey a, pointed apexes and almost no contrast. It is the type of the modernist programme, clean and optimistic, with a small x-height in the classic cuts.

skills.name: Neo-grotesque sans
skills.thesis: A typeface is a neutral vessel: it carries the message and adds nothing of its own.
skills.summary: The neutral sans of the grid: even widths, horizontal terminals, closed apertures, a large x-height and almost no contrast. It lets the layout speak and is the default voice of interfaces and corporate systems.

origin.note: Abner Peeler patents a paint distributor; the airbrush of Charles Burdick (1893) goes into photo studios for retouch.

adoptions.via: Streamline posters and car advertisements use airbrushed gradients and chrome.
Illustrators airbrush surreal chrome, lightning and X-ray cut-aways for album covers and magazines.
Photoshop 1.0 ships with an airbrush tool, and the soft spray becomes digital.
Web 2.0 logos take the airbrush gradient and the white specular highlight to the screen as glossy marks.
Apple Aqua icons in Mac OS X use soft gradients, highlights and cast shadows that echo airbrush work.
Glossy interface gradients and highlights take the airbrush look to the screen.

origin.note: Roman builders use the semicircular masonry arch at large scale in aqueducts, bridges and gates; the arch itself is older.

adoptions.via: Palladian arched windows and niches frame Georgian rooms.
Postmodern facades quote the round arch as a sign, not as a structure.
Arched mirrors, headboards, doorways and painted arches become a room motif.

origin.note: Three engineers in Recife patent the cobogó, a hollow concrete block for screen walls in a hot climate.

adoptions.via: Tropical modernism and desert houses in the United States use screen walls; Edward Durell Stone wraps the US Embassy in New Delhi (1959) in a pierced screen.
Breeze-block room dividers, bar fronts and planters move inside the house.

origin.note: The pen is older than print; Gutenberg cut his textura from the broad-nib book hand of the scribes, the first record of the pen in type.

adoptions.via: Gutenberg's textura for the 42-line Bible copies the broken broad-nib hand.
Nicolas Jenson cuts a roman with the diagonal stress of the humanist broad-nib hand.
Edward Johnston, a calligrapher, draws the London Underground sans from broad-nib proportions.

origin.note: Builders in northern Europe project the upper floors of timber houses beyond the lower floor on jetties.

adoptions.via: Frank Lloyd Wright carries the roofs of the Robie House 6 m past the wall on steel beams.
Mart Stam and then Marcel Breuer bend steel tube into a chair that has no back legs.
Wright cantilevers the concrete terraces of Fallingwater over a stream in Pennsylvania.

origin.note: Squares of two colours of marble pave Italian church floors and palace halls.

adoptions.via: Leon Battista Alberti builds the perspective of a picture on a squared pavement in De pictura.
Black and white floors pave Art Deco halls, bars and bathrooms.
Checker rugs, tiles and painted floors become a motif of colourful rooms.

origin.note: Italian painters model form with strong light and dark from the late 15th century; Caravaggio makes the contrast extreme in The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600).

adoptions.via: Caravaggio paints figures out of a dark ground with one hard shaft of light, and the Baroque painters follow.
Cecil B. DeMille and the cameraman Alvin Wyckoff light The Cheat with hard side light and call the result Rembrandt lighting.
The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari uses painted shadows and sharp light to set a mind in a distorted room.
Citizen Kane and The Maltese Falcon use low-key light, deep shadow and hard bars of light; crime films of the 1940s make it a house style.
Stills of noir films and press night photographs keep the single hard light and the black ground.
Blade Runner, shot by Jordan Cronenweth for Ridley Scott, cuts shafts of light through smoke and blinds in a colour city.

origin.note: Eadweard Muybridge records a galloping horse with a row of cameras; Étienne-Jules Marey takes many exposures on one plate from 1882.

adoptions.via: Étienne-Jules Marey makes his chronophotographic gun and fixed plate in Paris.
Anton Giulio Bragaglia publishes photodynamism, a blurred photograph of movement.
Giacomo Balla paints Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash with repeated legs and tail.
Marcel Duchamp paints Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2 in stages.

origin.note: Mario Bava lights Blood and Black Lace with red, green and blue gels; colour light is older in the theatre and in colour film.

adoptions.via: Mario Bava uses gelled light in Blood and Black Lace and sets the look of the giallo.
Dario Argento and the cameraman Luciano Tovoli light Suspiria with saturated gels and print it on dye-transfer Technicolor.
Nicolas Winding Refn bathes Only God Forgives in red and blue light.

origin.note: Albrecht Duerer publishes letters built with ruler and compass on a square grid in Underweysung der Messung.

adoptions.via: The committee of the Academie des Sciences draws the Romain du roi on a grid of 2304 small squares.
Paul Renner draws Futura from the circle, the square and the triangle.
Otl Aicher builds the pictograms of the Munich Olympics on a grid with angles of 45° and 90° only.
The Twitter bird is drawn from overlapping circles with set radii.
Material Design sets 24 dp icons with a 20 dp live area and keyline shapes.

origin.where: Horta de Ebro, La Roche-Guyon and Paris
origin.note: Picasso and Braque break objects into small flat planes in the first Cubist paintings.

adoptions.via: Picasso and Braque paint objects as flat planes in landscapes, Picasso at Horta de Ebro and Braque at La Roche-Guyon, and in the Paris still lifes.
Pavel Janak and Josef Gocar design Czech Cubist buildings with faceted walls, such as the House of the Black Madonna in Prague.
Bruno Taut builds the Glass Pavilion for the Werkbund exhibition in Cologne as a crystal dome of glass prisms.
Hermann Warm, Walter Reimann and Walter Roehrig build the angled, painted sets of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari.

origin.note: Kazimir Malevich shows tilted, floating shapes in Suprematist paintings at the exhibition 0.10.

adoptions.via: El Lissitzky draws Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge: a red wedge cuts into a white circle.
Aleksandr Rodchenko sets the lines of his posters, such as the Books ad, on strong diagonals.
Sergei Eisenstein stages frames of Battleship Potemkin along strong diagonals.
Jan Tschichold teaches the asymmetric, diagonal page in Die neue Typographie.

origin.note: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and co-authors publish the first diffusion method for images; it is a paper in machine learning.

adoptions.via: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel publish Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models.
Midjourney and DALL-E 2 put text-to-image models in the hands of illustrators and designers.
Stable Diffusion releases its weights in August, and its glossy default look spreads as a recognisable image style.

origin.note: Animators draw more frames at the start and the end of a move; Thomas and Johnston name it slow in and slow out.

adoptions.via: Robert Penner publishes easing equations for Flash, and web motion takes them up.
CSS transitions define timing functions such as ease-in-out and cubic-bezier().

origin.note: Egyptian carpenters lock the parts of chairs, beds and chests with mortise-and-tenon joints and leave the joints in view.

adoptions.via: Shaker joiners show dovetails and tenons on plain chests and chairs.
Gustav Stickley sells Craftsman furniture with through-tenons that show on the face.
Greene and Greene build the Gamble House in Pasadena with pegged and exposed timber joints.
Peter Zumthor and other critical regionalists keep the joint and the junction as the only ornament.

origin.note: George Albert Smith inserts magnified close views into Grandma's Reading Glass.

adoptions.via: Carl Theodor Dreyer fills the frame with the face of Renée Falconetti in The Passion of Joan of Arc.
Sergio Leone cuts between the eyes of gunmen and a wide desert in A Fistful of Dollars, on a Techniscope 2.35:1 frame.
Chuck Close paints a huge frontal head from a photograph in Big Self-Portrait (1967–68).

origin.note: The Sholes and Glidden typewriter by E. Remington and Sons moves the carriage one fixed step for each key, so its type must be monospaced.

adoptions.via: Typewriter faces, then Courier for IBM in 1955.
Video terminals such as the DEC VT100 draw the whole screen as a grid of 80 by 24 character cells.

origin.note: Greek Doric and Ionic columns carry vertical concave grooves; a Doric shaft has 20 flutes.

adoptions.via: Neoclassical and Regency furniture takes fluted and reeded legs and friezes.
Art Deco rooms use fluted pilasters, fluted glass and fluted wood panels.
Reeded glass and fluted wood or stone cover cabinets, islands and walls.

origin.note: Nam June Paik bends the picture of television sets with magnets in his first Exposition of Music-Electronic Television.

adoptions.via: Rosa Menkman writes the Glitch Studies Manifesto; designers copy channel splits and torn bands in posters and sites.

origin.note: Leon Battista Alberti describes a veil of threads that gives a grid over the scene in De pictura.

adoptions.via: Albrecht Dürer prints draughtsmen who draw through a frame with a grid in Underweysung der Messung.
Chuck Close works from a gridded photograph in Big Self-Portrait.

origin.note: Benjamin Day patents a mechanical tint of dots for printers; photographic halftone screens follow in the 1880s.

adoptions.via: The Daily Graphic of New York prints a photograph as a halftone.
Roy Lichtenstein paints enlarged Ben-Day dots by hand in Look Mickey.
Punk zines photocopy halftones until the dots break up.
Duotone icon sets print each glyph in two tones of one hue, as a two-screen duotone does in print.

origin.note: Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin shoot Chronique d'un été with the light synchronous-sound camera that Michel Brault operates by hand; earlier handheld shots exist.

adoptions.via: Raoul Coutard shoots À bout de souffle by hand for Jean-Luc Godard.
Rouch, Brault and the Direct Cinema crews carry the light 16mm camera and the sound recorder into real rooms.
The Dogme 95 Vow of Chastity demands that the camera is hand-held.
The Blair Witch Project gives the camera to its characters and shows the shake as their fear.
Andrew Bujalski shoots Funny Ha Ha with a small camera in plain rooms.
Sean Baker shoots Tangerine on three iPhone 5S phones with a clip-on anamorphic lens and a small stabiliser.

origin.note: William Farish publishes isometrical perspective as a method for engineering drawing.

adoptions.via: Theo van Doesburg and Cornelis van Eesteren show houses in axonometric drawings.
Isometric illustrations show products, data and offices on tech pages.
Icon packs for product pages and dashboards draw small objects on the isometric grid.

origin.note: Jean-Luc Godard cuts inside continuous shots in À bout de souffle and does not hide the jump.

adoptions.via: Video bloggers on YouTube cut the pauses out of a talk to the camera.
Vertical short-form apps make the fast jump cut the default rhythm of a clip.

origin.note: Ken Burns pans and zooms over still photographs in a documentary series; rostrum-camera moves are older.

adoptions.via: Apple names the pan-and-zoom setting after Burns in its photo and video software.

origin.note: Otto Hetzer patents glued laminated timber beams for halls and bridges.

adoptions.via: Alvar Aalto designs the Paimio chair with a frame of bent laminated birch.
Charles and Ray Eames put moulded plywood chairs into mass production.
Austrian researchers develop cross-laminated timber panels, and builders adopt them for floors and walls.
Waugh Thistleton builds Murray Grove in London, a 9-storey block with a CLT frame.

origin.note: Carvers cut the spaced roman capitals of the inscription on Trajan's Column.

adoptions.via: Fashion and hotel houses set their names in spaced roman capitals.
Carol Twombly draws the Trajan typeface for Adobe from the column inscription.
Luxury sites set spaced small-cap labels over a large serif head.

origin.note: Builders at Ain Ghazal coat floors and walls with burnt lime plaster; Catalhoyuk later paints its plastered walls.

adoptions.via: Le Corbusier records the white lime-washed houses of the Aegean on his Journey to the East.
Geoffrey Bawa builds white-plastered houses in Sri Lanka.
Beach houses in the USA put white-washed walls and boards in summer rooms.

origin.note: Goldsmiths engrave copper plates and print them as pictures; the method then spreads across Europe.

adoptions.via: George Bickham engraves the copperplate hands of The Universal Penman (1741) on copper.
John Baskerville has John Handy cut sharp, high-contrast roman type in Birmingham, and prints it on smooth wove paper.
Firmin Didot cuts roman type with hairline serifs and a vertical stress; Giambattista Bodoni follows in Parma.
Robert Thorne cuts fat faces that push the engraved contrast of the Didones to an extreme.
The UK Trade Marks Registration Act starts a register, and firms file engraved vignettes, banners and shaded figures.

origin.note: Alois Senefelder invents lithography in Bavaria.

adoptions.via: Odilon Redon publishes the lithographs of Dans le rêve, black dream visions.
Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec prints the poster Moulin Rouge: La Goulue in colour lithography.
Edvard Munch prints The Scream as a lithograph.

origin.note: Giorgio de Chirico paints empty squares with long raking shadows in The Mystery and Melancholy of a Street.

adoptions.via: F. W. Murnau casts the shadow of the vampire on the stairs in Nosferatu.
Surrealist painters take over the empty, shadowed scene of de Chirico.
Flat design adds a 45° long shadow to icons and buttons.
Surreal web scenes use long shadows on calm, empty grounds.

origin.note: Alfred Hitchcock shoots Rope in takes of about 10 minutes, the length of one reel, and hides each join in a dark back or a close shape.

adoptions.via: Orson Welles opens Touch of Evil with a single crane and tracking shot of about three minutes.
Béla Tarr cuts Sátántangó into 150 shots in 7 hours, many of them takes of several minutes.
Alexander Sokurov makes Russian Ark as one Steadicam take of 96 minutes through the Hermitage.
Birdman, shot by Emmanuel Lubezki, hides its cuts to look like one take.
1917, shot by Roger Deakins, joins a few long takes into the look of one shot.

origin.note: Graphic matches are older; the reference case is Stanley Kubrick's cut from a thrown bone to a satellite in orbit.

adoptions.via: Material motion in Android 5.0 carries one element from screen to screen as a shared-element transition.

origin.note: Josef Mueller-Brockmann and the journal Neue Grafik (1958) spread the modular grid for posters and print.

adoptions.via: Otl Aicher builds the corporate design of Lufthansa on a fixed grid of marks, type and colour.
Unimark issues the New York City Transit Graphics Standards Manual, with sign grids for the whole system.
Bootstrap 2.0 ships a 12 column fluid grid for web pages.

origin.note: Disney's multiplane camera moves painted glass layers at different speeds; The Old Mill (1937) is its first film.

adoptions.via: Parallax scroll pages move the background layers slower than the page.
Layered app icons on tvOS, and later visionOS, tilt their layers with parallax.

origin.note: Georges Claude shows his neon tube at the Paris Motor Show in 1910, and a Paris hairdresser installs a neon sign in 1912.

adoptions.via: Venturi, Scott Brown and Izenour study the neon signs of the Las Vegas Strip in Learning from Las Vegas.
Ridley Scott fills the wet night streets of Blade Runner with neon signs.
Web designers fake neon with layered text-shadow and box-shadow glows once browsers support CSS3.

origin.note: Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrates linear perspective; Alberti writes the method down in De pictura (1435).

adoptions.via: Cassette Futurism screens and sleeves draw wireframe floors to a horizon.
Tron draws vector grids that run to a horizon.
Vaporwave draws neon grid floors under a sunset.

origin.note: Raoul Hausmann and Hannah Höch of Berlin Dada cut press photographs and paste them into one sheet.

adoptions.via: Alexander Rodchenko and El Lissitzky use photomontage in Constructivist posters and books.
Sergei Eisenstein carries the collision of fragments into the cut of Strike and Battleship Potemkin.
Punk zines and record sleeves cut up newspapers with scissors and glue.
Photoshop makes the cut and the layer digital; early cyberculture prints dense photo-illustration.
Designers cut photographs of objects and clouds into collage scenes, in the line of the Surrealist collages of Max Ernst.

origin.note: Ken Knowlton writes BEFLIX, a language that draws computer films as grids of cells in a small set of grey tones.

adoptions.via: The Xerox Alto has a bitmap display, and its programs draw icons cell by cell.
Susan Kare draws the Macintosh icons and the Chicago bitmap face on a grid of 32 by 32 cells.
Zuzana Licko draws the Emigre bitmap faces for the 72 dpi screen and the dot-matrix printer.
The eBoy group publishes pixel illustrations of cities and objects on the web.

origin.note: George Bickham's The Universal Penman engraves the roundhand of the English writing masters, the model for every later formal script.

adoptions.via: Engraved copybooks of the writing masters, then metal scripts that copy the plates.
Frank Mason Robinson writes the Coca-Cola wordmark in Spencerian, a pointed-pen hand.

origin.note: The inscription at the base of Trajan's Column sets the model for Roman capitals.

adoptions.via: Nicolas Jenson prints in Venice with a roman face whose capitals follow Roman inscriptions.
Edward Johnston draws the London Underground block letters on the proportions of Roman capitals.
Hermann Zapf releases Optima, a sans serif whose shapes come from stone inscriptions he saw in Florence.

origin.note: Claude Monet shows a group of Haystacks canvases, each of one motif in a different light.

adoptions.via: Frank Stella starts his Black Paintings, in which equal stripes repeat the shape of the canvas.
Bernd and Hilla Becher begin their typologies of water towers, blast furnaces and houses on one fixed frame.
Andy Warhol repeats one soup can or one face in a grid of identical canvases.

origin.note: Carlo Scarpa separates new steel and stone from the old walls with narrow joints in the Castelvecchio museum (1957 to 1964).

adoptions.via: Carlo Scarpa finishes the Castelvecchio in Verona; each new element touches the old fabric along a visible gap.
John Pawson and Claudio Silvestrin set plaster and doors flush, with recessed joints in place of trim.
Peter Zumthor and other critical regionalists use the shadow line between materials as their detail.

origin.note: Greek vase painters fill figures with black slip and scratch the detail.

adoptions.via: Cut black paper profiles become a fashion in France and take the name of the minister Etienne de Silhouette.
Lotte Reiniger shows The Adventures of Prince Achmed, a feature film of cut paper silhouettes.
Otl Aicher draws the Munich Olympic pictograms as white-on-colour figure silhouettes.
Font Awesome 1.0 gives the web a free set of solid glyphs in an icon font.

origin.note: Helen Frankenthaler pours thinned oil on raw canvas in Mountains and Sea.

adoptions.via: Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland visit the studio of Frankenthaler and take up the stain method; Louis turns it into his Veils from 1954.
Noland moves from oil to thinned acrylic, which stains the cloth with no halo; Louis stains with thinned Magna acrylic from the first Veils in 1954.

origin.note: Disney animators exaggerate the volume of a ball and a face; Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston name it the first of twelve principles in 1981.

adoptions.via: John Lasseter applies it to computer animation in Luxo Jr. and in his SIGGRAPH paper of 1987.
Spring-damped animation in iOS 7 lets interface elements overshoot and settle.
3D motion design renders soft bodies that wobble, inflate and bounce.

origin.note: Rays from a half disc appear on Art Deco facades, gates and lift doors around the Paris exposition of decorative arts in 1925.

adoptions.via: Art Deco furniture, screens and mirrors take the ray motif inside.
George Nelson Associates design ray-form wall clocks for Howard Miller; the starburst mirror follows in the 1950s.
Space Age signs, packaging and posters use starbursts as a sign of the future.
Neo-deco rooms bring back the fan and the sunburst in brass and glass.

origin.note: Venetian workers set marble offcuts in lime and polish the floor of palaces: terrazzo alla veneziana.

adoptions.via: Poured terrazzo with brass strips paves Art Deco lobbies.
Poured terrazzo floors go into mid-century homes, schools and airports.
Terrazzo moves from the floor to tables, tiles, lamps and small objects.

origin.note: Theodor Scheimpflug patents the rule for tilted lens and plane of focus.

adoptions.via: Group f/64 use large-format view cameras with small stops and sharp focus from front to back.
Julius Shulman photographs Case Study House No. 22 on a large-format camera with upright lines.
Nikon sells the PC-Nikkor 35mm f/3.5, the first shift lens for a 35mm camera.
Photoshop CS6 adds the Tilt-Shift blur filter, and the miniature look spreads on the web.

origin.note: Victor Horta uses curved iron stems on the stair and the ceiling of the Hotel Tassel.

adoptions.via: Hermann Obrist shows the Cyclamen wall hanging, an embroidery of one long curved stem.
Jugend and Pan magazines print initials and vignettes in interlaced curved lines.
Otto Eckmann draws the Eckmann-Schrift with brush-like curved strokes.
Hector Guimard designs the iron entrances of the Paris Metro with plant-like curves.

origin.note: Darius Wells makes wood type in quantity with a routing machine, and the poster printers take it up at once.

adoptions.via: The first wood type lines are fat faces copied from the London founders.
Wood type founders add Egyptian slabs and condensed letters for posters.
Trade cards and shop signs set the name of the firm in heavy wood letters.

origin.note: The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the oldest dated printed book made from woodblocks.

adoptions.via: Suzuki Harunobu and his printers make the full-colour nishiki-e print on many blocks.
Paul Gauguin cuts the woodcuts of the Noa Noa series with flat colour and rough cuts.
Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff of Die Brücke cut jagged woodcuts in Dresden.
